paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when an algorithm can evaluate a noisy objective but does not receive its gradient directly. The setting is stochastic convex minimization: the goal is to find a low objective value despite randomness in the available evaluations. The authors introduce POEM, a parameter-free method designed for this setting.

POEM combines two adaptive choices. Its step-size rule uses distance together with finite differences, which estimate changes in the objective from function evaluations. It also adapts a smoothing parameter. These mechanisms address central choices in zeroth-order optimization: how to extract useful directional information from evaluations and how far to move using that information.

The theoretical result concerns oracle complexity, meaning the number of objective queries needed to reach a desired optimization accuracy. The authors show that POEM is near optimal by this measure. Numerical experiments also report better performance than existing zeroth-order methods. Together, these findings support both the method’s theoretical efficiency in the stated convex setting and its practical promise in the tested problems.
icml-2025-a-parameter-free-and-near-opti.tldr: POEM adapts its optimization steps and smoothing to achieve near-optimal query complexity for stochastic convex optimization without gradients.

paragraphs: A backdoor in a reinforcement learning agent aims to produce two behaviors: normal task performance during training and an attacker-chosen response when a trigger appears during deployment. Earlier attacks often depended on rewards outside the environment’s legitimate range. The authors show why that matters: enforcing the proper reward constraints can make those attacks fail.

The paper introduces inception attacks, which manipulate training data while respecting strict reward constraints. At a conceptual level, they alter the association between past observations, successful actions, and the attacker’s desired behavior. This shifts the source of the backdoor from extreme reward values to misleading relationships within the experience used for learning.

The authors formally define this attack class and prove that it can achieve both adversarial objectives against arbitrary Markov decision processes within their framework. They also develop an online attack that reaches 100% attack success across multiple tested environments while minimally affecting task performance. The empirical result shows that reward restrictions alone did not prevent backdoors in those evaluations.
icml-2025-adversarial-inception-backdoor.tldr: Inception attacks demonstrate that reinforcement learning backdoors can remain effective even when training rewards obey strict constraints.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference represents uncertainty through a posterior distribution rather than returning only one fitted answer. This paper asks whether transformers can perform that richer form of inference through in-context learning. In this setting, the model uses information supplied in its context without undergoing additional training for the particular inference problem.

The authors introduce a framework combining ideas from prior fitted networks and continuous normalizing flows. Its purpose is to produce samples from complex posterior distributions for commonly used statistical models. The examples covered include generalized linear models and latent factor models, extending the investigation beyond obtaining a single prediction or parameter estimate.

Experiments on real-world datasets find that the resulting posterior samples have quality similar to those produced by leading Markov chain Monte Carlo and variational inference methods. Those comparison methods do not operate in context. The result supports the possibility of learning a reusable inference procedure inside a transformer, with demonstrated posterior quality for the statistical models and datasets studied.
icml-2025-can-transformers-learn-full-ba.tldr: A transformer framework performs Bayesian inference in context, producing posterior samples comparable in quality to established inference methods in experiments.

paragraphs: CN-Diff is a generative approach to time-series forecasting that changes how a diffusion model prepares data for generation. The paper focuses on nonlinear transformations and learnable conditioning in the forward process. These additions are intended to help the model represent complex patterns in time series before it learns to reverse that process.

The authors derive both the forward and reverse processes and introduce a corresponding training loss. They report that the richer forward construction simplifies the reverse process. The learned condition also helps establish an efficient prior distribution and reduces the gap between the true negative log-likelihood and the variational approximation used in the framework.

The practical evaluation covers nine real-world datasets, where CN-Diff outperforms other leading time-series models. Ablation studies examine the contribution of its individual components. The combined message is that forecasting improvements can come from redesigning the diffusion process and its training objective together, with the reported gains supported across the evaluated datasets rather than a single forecasting example.
icml-2025-conditional-diffusion-model-wi.tldr: CN-Diff improves time-series forecasting by adding nonlinear transformations and learned conditions to a diffusion model’s forward process.

paragraphs: Counterfactual image generation asks how an image would change under an intervention governed by a causal model. Producing a convincing result requires more than visual quality: the edit should follow the intended causal relationship while retaining relevant aspects of the original image’s identity. The paper treats these requirements as connected parts of the generation problem.

The authors introduce diffusion-based causal mechanisms and three notions of abduction: spatial, semantic, and dynamic. Their general framework brings semantic representations into diffusion models using Pearlian causal reasoning. Here, abduction concerns reasoning from an observed image about the underlying information needed to construct a counterfactual version of that same observation.

The central contribution is explicit control over high-level semantic identity during counterfactual editing. The authors demonstrate that semantic control supports principled trade-offs between preserving identity and following causal interventions faithfully. They describe this treatment of semantic identity in diffusion counterfactuals as a first to their knowledge. The result frames identity preservation as something to reason about and balance, rather than simply assume from realistic-looking images.
icml-2025-diffusion-counterfactual-gener.tldr: This framework uses semantic representations in diffusion models to balance causal faithfulness and identity preservation during counterfactual image editing.

paragraphs: The paper uses independent component analysis, or ICA, as a simplified model of feature learning. Its motivation is that filters learned by ICA resemble first-layer filters learned by deep convolutional networks on natural images. Because ICA searches for strongly non-Gaussian projections, it provides a way to examine how input structure interacts with the optimization algorithm.

On a simple synthetic data model, the authors prove that FastICA needs at least roughly d to the fourth power samples to recover one non-Gaussian direction from d-dimensional inputs. Vanilla online stochastic gradient descent performs better. With data-dependent smoothing of the loss, they prove that the optimal sample complexity of roughly d squared can be reached.

These results show that finding the same underlying feature can require very different amounts of data depending on the optimization procedure. The paper also identifies a search phase for FastICA on ImageNet and discusses how the strong non-Gaussian structure of natural images compensates for its poor sample complexity. The synthetic guarantees and image observations together connect algorithmic difficulty with the strength of structure present in data.
icml-2025-feature-learning-from-non-gaus.tldr: An ICA analysis shows how optimization choices and non-Gaussian data structure jointly determine the sample requirements of feature learning.

paragraphs: Scale-wise autoregressive image generation builds an image by predicting successive scales, preserving its two-dimensional organization. The paper identifies two obstacles in the earlier VAR approach: a complicated scale schedule and tight coupling between the generator and a matching discrete tokenizer. Together, these make next-scale prediction less general and tokenizer updates less flexible.

FlowAR replaces that structure with a simple rule: each successive scale doubles the previous one. This removes the need for VAR’s specialized multiscale residual tokenizer and allows the framework to use an off-the-shelf variational autoencoder. The simplified organization also enables the authors to integrate flow matching into the image-generation process.

On ImageNet-256, the authors report better generation performance than previous methods. The significance extends to how the system is assembled: simplifying the scale structure reduces dependence on a particular tokenizer design while supporting high-quality synthesis. The paper therefore presents both an architectural change toward more modular image generation and an empirical demonstration of its effectiveness on the stated benchmark.
icml-2025-flowar-scale-wise-autoregressi.tldr: FlowAR combines a simpler next-scale image generator with flow matching, enabling flexible VAE use and improved ImageNet-256 generation.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether flexible, goal-directed behavior requires an agent to learn how its environment works. It addresses the question formally by connecting generalization across multistep goals with predictive knowledge of the environment. The relevant capability is achieving goals through sequences of actions, where consequences extend beyond the next immediate step.

The authors show that an agent capable of this form of generalization must have learned a predictive world model. They also show that the model can be extracted from the agent’s policy, the mechanism that determines its actions. This connects an agent’s ability to act successfully with environmental knowledge recoverable from that ability.

The result further links stronger performance and more complex achievable goals to increasingly accurate world models. Its implications include studying safe general agents, placing bounds on capabilities in complex environments, and developing methods to elicit predictive models from policies. The contribution is a formal relationship between specified goal-directed capabilities and learned environmental prediction, rather than an empirical comparison of particular agent architectures.
icml-2025-general-agents-need-world-mode.tldr: The paper formally shows that generalizing to multistep goal-directed tasks requires predictive environmental knowledge recoverable from an agent’s policy.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms often depend on parameters whose useful settings change as a search progresses. This paper studies how to adjust those parameters dynamically for evolutionary algorithms tackling multiple objectives in combinatorial problems. The challenge is to represent the evolving search well enough for a reinforcement learning controller to make useful configuration decisions.

The authors formulate configuration as a Markov decision process and represent the convergence of candidate solutions in objective space using a graph. A graph neural network learns embeddings of that graph, enriching the state information available to the controller. This makes the arrangement of solutions across objectives part of the evidence used to update algorithm parameters.

Experiments across diverse multi-objective combinatorial problems report better effectiveness and adaptability than traditional and reinforcement learning configuration methods. The approach also shows favorable generalization across objective types and problem sizes, with applicability to different evolutionary methods. These findings support graph-based search representations as a useful foundation for adaptive configuration across the tested optimization settings.
icml-2025-graph-supported-dynamic-algori.tldr: A graph-based reinforcement learning controller adapts evolutionary algorithm parameters using the evolving distribution of solutions across multiple objectives.

paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model adapt from demonstrations without changing its parameters, but poisoned examples can also introduce backdoor behavior. This paper proposes a dual-learning hypothesis: a model can infer both the intended task concept and a malicious backdoor concept from the same demonstrations. Both then influence its output probabilities.

The authors derive an upper bound on backdoor effects that identifies the preference ratio between task and backdoor concepts as the dominant factor in vulnerability. This analysis motivates ICLShield, which uses confidence and similarity scores to encourage selection of clean demonstrations. Its defense strategy is to adjust which inferred concept has greater influence during in-context learning.

Experiments across multiple models and tasks report state-of-the-art defense effectiveness, with an average improvement of 26.02% over existing approaches. The method also demonstrates adaptability and defensive performance with closed-source models, including GPT-4. These results connect a theoretical account of competing concepts to a practical demonstration-selection defense, with effectiveness established in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-iclshield-exploring-and-mitiga.tldr: ICLShield uses confidence and similarity to favor clean demonstrations, reducing backdoor effects linked to competing task and malicious concepts.

paragraphs: Inverse optimization learns an optimization-based explanation for observed input-decision pairs. Most previous work learns what objective a decision maker appears to optimize. This paper instead learns the feasible region: the constraints defining which decisions are available. It studies this problem with a known linear objective, placing the learning burden on the constraints.

The authors introduce two training losses and a parameterized class of constraint functions. This representation can naturally capture discontinuous changes in decisions as inputs vary, exceeding the representational ability of the previous objective-only method. Learning constraints produces nonconvex training problems, so the paper develops a tailored block coordinate descent algorithm with smoothing.

For more restricted hypothesis classes, the authors also reformulate training as a tractable convex program or a mixed integer linear program. Synthetic experiments and two power-system applications, including comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches, validate the proposal. The contribution is both representational and computational: learning what is feasible broadens the behaviors inverse optimization can explain, while specialized formulations make that learning approachable.
icml-2025-inverse-optimization-via-learn.tldr: The paper learns constraints for known linear objectives, enabling inverse optimization to capture discontinuous decisions and supporting tailored training algorithms.

paragraphs: Multi-view graph clustering groups nodes using several views of their features and relationships. A central difficulty is combining node information with graph structure when connected nodes may be similar or dissimilar. These two patterns, called homophily and heterophily, create different demands on graph neural networks and on learning representations that agree across views.

The paper introduces Node-Guided Contrastive Encoding, or NGCE. Its key choice is to let node features guide embedding generation. The authors describe this guidance as improving compatibility with graph neural network filtering, integrating information from both homophilic and heterophilic structures, and strengthening the contrastive learning process that connects representations across views.

Experiments on six multi-view benchmark datasets demonstrate robust performance across both graph types. The finding matters because a clustering representation must reconcile what a node looks like with how it connects to others, and those signals need not align in the same way everywhere. NGCE provides a feature-guided approach to that reconciliation, supported by the reported benchmark evaluations.
icml-2025-multi-view-graph-clustering-vi.tldr: NGCE uses node features to guide contrastive graph representations, supporting clustering across views with both similar and dissimilar connected nodes.

paragraphs: Federated learning coordinates training across machines, but those machines may participate in only some rounds. This paper studies how to preserve differential privacy under that partial-participation pattern. Earlier methods achieved optimal performance and efficiency when all machines participated, yet did not extend effectively to the more flexible participation setting considered here.

The authors introduce a noise-cancellation mechanism designed to preserve privacy while retaining convergence rates and computational efficiency. The mechanism addresses the interaction between privacy protection and intermittent participation. Its role is to make privacy-preserving optimization work efficiently when the set of participating machines changes across training rounds.

The analysis is carried out within stochastic convex optimization and establishes optimal performance for both homogeneous and heterogeneous data distributions. Thus, the stated guarantee covers settings where machines have similar data as well as settings where their distributions differ. The contribution broadens the participation conditions under which efficient, differentially private federated optimization is supported, with the optimality claims belonging to the paper’s convex optimization framework.
icml-2025-privacy-preserving-federated-c.tldr: A noise-cancellation mechanism enables optimal differentially private federated convex optimization when machines participate in only some training rounds.

paragraphs: Sampling from an unnormalized density requires generating representative samples without knowing the distribution’s full normalization. Neural samplers aim to learn a reusable generator, while parallel tempering is an established Markov chain Monte Carlo approach. The paper highlights their different strengths: parallel tempering uses target evaluations efficiently, whereas a trained neural sampler can supply fresh samples without rerunning that procedure.

The proposed Progressive Tempering Sampler with Diffusion trains diffusion models sequentially across temperatures. It combines higher-temperature models to generate approximate samples for a lower temperature. Those samples receive limited MCMC refinement and then train the next diffusion model, allowing information gathered at earlier temperature levels to support later ones.

The authors report well-mixed, uncorrelated samples and a substantial improvement in target-evaluation efficiency over diffusion-based neural samplers. The central idea is to reuse sampling information across temperatures while building a generator that remains useful afterward. The reported comparison supports improvements over neural sampling alternatives; the abstract does not claim that the method surpasses parallel tempering itself.
icml-2025-progressive-tempering-sampler-.tldr: The sampler trains diffusion models across temperatures, reusing and refining samples to improve target-evaluation efficiency over diffusion-based neural samplers.

paragraphs: Predicting molecular properties requires accounting for interactions among groups of atoms, not just isolated pairs. Existing graph and attention models often approximate interactions involving three or four atoms through message passing or restrict direct attention to triplets. The paper argues that these choices make higher-order interactions difficult to represent directly and efficiently.

MABNet introduces a geometric attention framework that allows groups of four atoms to communicate directly. This quartet-level operation is designed specifically to model four-body interactions. By changing the unit of interaction, the framework bypasses computational bottlenecks associated with traditional triplet-based attention while retaining an explicit connection to many-body molecular physics.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on benchmarks including MD22 and SPICE, supporting the model’s ability to capture complex interactions in large molecules. These findings motivate its use in molecular simulation relevant to drug design and materials discovery. The framework is also described as extensible toward higher-order quantum effects, which is a direction enabled by its design rather than a separate demonstrated benchmark result.
icml-2025-quadruple-attention-in-many-bo.tldr: MABNet directly models four-atom interactions with geometric attention, achieving state-of-the-art molecular prediction results on MD22 and SPICE.

paragraphs: Reward models assign scores intended to reflect human preferences, but a score does not reveal which response attributes caused it. RATE addresses this by estimating how attributes such as sentiment, helpfulness, or complexity affect the reward. Its target is a causal effect: what changing an attribute does to the score, rather than how that attribute merely correlates with it.

The method uses language models to rewrite responses into counterfactual examples. A difficulty is that a rewrite may change more than the intended attribute, creating substantial bias in the estimated effect. RATE’s central idea is to rewrite twice and use that construction to adjust for the influence of imperfect rewriting.

The paper establishes the validity of the procedure and provides empirical evidence that it estimates effects effectively. This matters because counterfactual text edits are useful for probing reward models only when unintended changes are accounted for. RATE turns the imperfection of generated rewrites into an explicit estimation problem, providing a way to examine what a reward model actually favors.
icml-2025-rate-causal-explainability-of-.tldr: RATE estimates the causal effect of response attributes on reward scores by using a second rewrite to adjust for imperfect counterfactual edits.

paragraphs: Comment-ranking systems can promote civility or other forms of conversational quality, but their choices also determine which viewpoints receive attention. The paper examines a tension in this process: improving discussion quality can inadvertently make legitimate perspectives less visible. Its goal is to build representation guarantees into ranking instead of leaving viewpoint inclusion as an incidental outcome.

The authors adapt justified representation, a concept from social choice, to the comment-ranking setting. They incorporate it as a constraint on the ranking procedure. This gives representation a formal role alongside the platform’s other objectives, so the ranking must account for more than whichever comments score highest on engagement or quality alone.

The paper finds that enforcing this constraint increases the inclusion of diverse viewpoints while remaining compatible with optimizing engagement or conversational quality. The finding supports treating representation as a design requirement within ranking systems. It does not require abandoning other ranking goals; it provides a formal way to pursue those goals while imposing a specific guarantee about whose perspectives are represented.
icml-2025-representative-ranking-for-del.tldr: Adding justified-representation constraints to comment rankings increases viewpoint inclusion while remaining compatible with engagement and discussion-quality objectives.

paragraphs: Model editing changes a language model’s responses after training. Adapter-based approaches can apply edits when a prompt resembles a target in representation space, avoiding direct changes to the model’s weights. This paper identifies a major weakness in existing adapters: shared words can trigger an edit even when the prompt is unrelated to its intended meaning.

Projector Editor Networks for Model Editing, or PENME, learns a representation space designed to distinguish semantic relevance from lexical overlap. Irrelevant prompts are kept apart, while paraphrases remain close together. This arrangement aims to localize edits precisely, making the decision to apply an edit depend on the relevant meaning rather than superficial word similarity.

The empirical study reports state-of-the-art model-editing performance, greater inference efficiency than previous methods, and adaptability across architectures. These findings connect representation quality directly to editing reliability. The contribution addresses where an edit should apply as well as whether it produces the desired response, reducing the chance that an otherwise valid edit spills into unrelated prompts.
icml-2025-resolving-lexical-bias-in-mode.tldr: PENME learns representations that separate irrelevant word-overlapping prompts from true paraphrases, improving the precision and efficiency of model editing.

paragraphs: STAMP helps content creators and benchmark curators determine whether their material entered a language model’s pretraining data. Its approach requires preparing content before publication. For each original item, the framework creates several rephrasings with distinct secret-key watermarks, releases one version publicly, and retains the others as private comparison material.

Later, the creator compares the model’s likelihoods for the public and private versions using paired statistical tests. The comparison uses related versions of the same content to assess dataset membership. This provides a structured basis for evidence about inclusion, while the authors also verify that the rephrasing process preserves the original material’s meaning and utility.

The evaluation detects contamination across four benchmarks that each appear only once in training and together constitute less than 0.001% of the total tokens. STAMP outperforms several contamination-detection and dataset-inference baselines. Two real-world applications also confirm inclusion of paper abstracts and blog articles, supporting the method’s usefulness beyond the benchmark contamination experiments.
icml-2025-stamp-your-content-proving-dat.tldr: STAMP compares model likelihoods for public and private watermarked rephrasings to detect whether a dataset was included in pretraining.

paragraphs: A language model can produce different answers to the same input, so comparing two responses cannot reliably establish whether an intervention changed its behavior. Comparing complete output distributions is computationally impractical. This paper develops a statistical framework for distinguishing intervention-related response changes from the variation already present in a stochastic system.

The method repeatedly samples outputs and represents them in a low-dimensional space based on semantic similarity. It constructs empirical distributions for the null and alternative hypotheses, enabling frequentist tests without restrictive distributional assumptions. The framework works with black-box models and supports arbitrary input perturbations as well as interventions such as changing the model variant.

Its outputs include interpretable p-values and scalar effect sizes, separating evidence for a change from a measure of its magnitude. It also controls error rates when testing multiple perturbations. Case studies demonstrate quantifying response changes, measuring true and false positive rates, and assessing alignment with reference models. The contribution is a tractable statistical basis for auditing response behavior across repeated generations.
icml-2025-statistical-hypothesis-testing.tldr: The framework tests whether interventions change a language model’s response distribution using repeated sampling and low-dimensional semantic comparisons.

paragraphs: Reward-guided generation steers a language model toward preferred responses during inference without further training the base model. Existing methods can be expensive because they score candidate next tokens separately. They also commonly use reward models trained on complete responses, even though generation requires choosing how to extend an unfinished sequence.

The paper introduces a reward-model architecture trained with a Bradley–Terry loss to prefer the optimal sequence expansion. A single call produces scores for every candidate token at a generation step. This addresses both the cost of repeated scoring and the mismatch between evaluating completed text and selecting the next continuation.

The authors theoretically analyze reward-guided methods and show that earlier techniques prefer suboptimal sequences compared with their method during inference. Experiments report substantially faster inference through fewer reward-model calls, with performance competitive with previous reward-guided methods and offline reinforcement learning from human feedback. The result supports improving preference-guided decoding by redesigning what the reward model predicts at each step.
icml-2025-towards-cost-effective-reward-.tldr: A reward model scores all next-token candidates in one call, making preference-guided generation faster while retaining competitive performance.

paragraphs: Understanding which examples a model memorizes can help investigate data quality, privacy, and generalization. This paper introduces Cumulative Sample Loss, or CSL, as a computationally inexpensive proxy for memorization. For each training example, CSL accumulates its loss throughout training, capturing its learning history rather than only its loss at the end.

The authors find high cosine similarity between CSL and stability-based memorization estimates. They also establish theoretical connections: low CSL implies nontrivial bounds on stability-based memorization and learning time. These results give the accumulated training signal both empirical support and a formal relationship to the more expensive quantity it is intended to approximate.

The paper reports that CSL is four orders of magnitude cheaper to compute than the stability-based method and can be obtained without additional training overhead. Applications include finding mislabeled examples and detecting duplicates, where the metric achieves state-of-the-art performance. The contribution makes memorization-related analysis accessible through information already generated during training, while retaining the distinction between a proxy and the underlying memorization measure.
icml-2025-towards-memorization-estimatio.tldr: Cumulative Sample Loss offers a cheap, theoretically supported proxy for memorization and performs strongly at identifying mislabeled and duplicate examples.

paragraphs: Direct preference alignment methods train language models from preferences, but the growing number of loss functions makes their relationships difficult to understand. This paper develops a conceptual and technical framework for interpreting those losses. Its central question is whether an existing preference objective can be translated into a symbolic program that characterizes its semantics.

The authors formalize preference losses as discrete reasoning problems. Their framework covers approaches involving a single model as well as those using a reference model, and they identify symbolic forms for several common variants. This provides a shared language for describing objectives that otherwise appear as separate mathematical proposals.

The formal view reveals structure in the space of possible preference losses and supports rigorous comparisons among existing methods. It also allows new losses to be derived systematically from first principles. The contribution is therefore a way to reason about and design preference objectives, with the stated aim of guiding alignment research rather than a reported claim that one new objective universally performs best.
icml-2025-understanding-the-logic-of-dir.tldr: A symbolic logic framework characterizes direct preference losses, clarifies their relationships, and enables systematic derivation of new objectives.

paragraphs: When a pretrained model receives a new checkpoint, specialized fine-tuning performed on an older version may need to be repeated. This paper investigates transferring that specialization without training again or accessing training data. It represents the fine-tuning changes as a task vector: the modifications made relative to the original base model.

The approach adapts model re-basin techniques to transformers, using weight permutations to align the task vector with a new backbone. Residual connections and multi-head attention create structural challenges for this alignment. The proposed method uses two levels grounded in spectral theory, first permuting attention heads and then adjusting parameters within selected pairs of heads.

Experiments on visual and textual tasks demonstrate transfer of fine-tuned knowledge to new pretrained backbones without any training steps or datapoints. The significance is that specialization can be carried forward through parameter alignment in the evaluated settings. This offers a route to benefiting from an updated base model while reusing work already encoded in an older model’s fine-tuning changes.
icml-2025-update-your-transformer-to-the.tldr: Transformer-specific weight alignment transfers fine-tuning changes to updated pretrained checkpoints without additional training or data in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Deciding when to retrain requires balancing the expense of updating a model against the cost of leaving a degrading model in service. The paper considers a difficult practical setting: only a few examples are available, distribution shifts have unknown effects, and the relative costs of retraining and poor performance are hard to specify.

The authors formulate retraining as a decision problem and propose an uncertainty-based method that continually forecasts how model performance will evolve. Performance is evaluated using a bounded metric. This makes anticipated performance and its uncertainty central to the decision, addressing a gap in shift detection alone, which does not account for the cost trade-off.

Experiments on classification tasks across seven datasets show consistent improvements over existing baselines. The authors also assess robustness when cost trade-offs vary and when those trade-offs are misspecified. These findings support forecasting performance as a useful basis for retraining decisions under limited information, with the empirical evidence coming from the classification settings evaluated in the paper.
icml-2025-when-to-retrain-a-machine-lear.tldr: An uncertainty-based method forecasts model performance to decide when retraining is worthwhile, outperforming baselines across seven classification datasets.
